analysis.paraphrase_effect_summary: Both correct and equivalent. The wording chose only the surface form: '$e^{3x}$' produced exponentials with multiples in the exponent, while the prose's device of naming $u$ for the exponential produced powers of a single Real.exp - effectively doing the substitution in the paraphrase rather than in the proof. Whether the integral got a let-bound name likewise tracked whether the paraphrase named it, the same pattern as gpt:67, gpt:403 and gpt:456.

rigorous_paraphrase: Let $c>0$ be a real number; prove that there exists a labeling $f:\mathbb{Z}^2\to\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ of the lattice points such that the set of values $\{f(P):P\in\mathbb{Z}^2\}$ is finite and such that for every $i$ in the range of $f$ and every pair of points $P,Q\in\mathbb{Z}^2$ (not necessarily distinct) with $f(P)=f(Q)=i$ one has $\sqrt{(x_Q-x_P)^2+(y_Q-y_P)^2}\ge c^{\,i}$, if and only if $c<\sqrt{2}$. Prove that the answer is $c<\sqrt{2}$.
nonrigorous_paraphrase: For a positive real number $c$, prove that one can attach a positive whole-number label to every lattice point of the plane in such a way that only finitely many different labels are ever used and, for each label that occurs, any two lattice points carrying that label, not necessarily distinct from each other, are at Euclidean distance at least $c$ raised to the power of that label, exactly when $c$ is smaller than the square root of two. Prove that the answer is $c<\sqrt{2}$.
rigorous_formalization: theorem lattice_labeling_iff (c : ℝ) (hc : 0 < c) : (∃ f : ℤ × ℤ → ℕ, (∀ P, 0 < f P) ∧ (Set.range f).Finite ∧ ∀ i ∈ Set.range f, ∀ P Q : ℤ × ℤ, f P = i → f Q = i → c ^ i ≤ Real.sqrt (((Q.1 : ℝ) - (P.1 : ℝ)) ^ 2 + ((Q.2 : ℝ) - (P.2 : ℝ)) ^ 2)) ↔ c < Real.sqrt 2 := by sorry
nonrigorous_formalization: theorem lattice_labeling_iff_lt_sqrt_two (c : ℝ) (hc : 0 < c) : (∃ label : ℤ × ℤ → ℕ, Set.Finite (Set.range label) ∧ (∀ p, 0 < label p) ∧ ∀ p q, p ≠ q → label p = label q → c ^ label p ≤ Real.sqrt ((((p.1 - q.1 : ℤ) : ℝ) ^ 2) + (((p.2 - q.2 : ℤ) : ℝ) ^ 2))) ↔ c < Real.sqrt 2 := by sorry
reference: theorem omni_theorem_3965 (c : ℝ) (hc : 0 < c) : (∃ f : ℤ × ℤ → ℕ, (∀ x y : ℤ, f (x, y) > 0) ∧ Set.Finite {i | ∃ x y : ℤ, f (x, y) = i} ∧ ∀ i ∈ Set.range f, ∀ x1 x2 y1 y2 : ℤ, (f (x1, y1) = i ∧ f (x2, y2) = i) → c ^ i ≤ Real.sqrt ((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2)) ↔ c < Real.sqrt 2 := by sorry

differences.description: A imposes the distance condition on every pair of points with the same label, including a point paired with itself, as the paraphrase's parenthetical requires. B restricts it to distinct points via p != q.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: Rigorous: 'every pair of points $P,Q\in\mathbb{Z}^2$ (not necessarily distinct)' places the parenthetical immediately at the quantifier, where A could not miss it. Non-rigorous: 'any two lattice points carrying that label, not necessarily distinct from each other' relocates it to the end of the noun phrase, after an intervening participial phrase, and B dropped it.

differences.description: A keeps the outer layer 'for every i in the range of f' and conditions on f P = i and f Q = i; B drops that layer, using label p = label q directly with the exponent label p.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: Rigorous: 'for every $i$ in the range of $f$ and every pair of points ... with $f(P)=f(Q)=i$' names the label, which A carried; the prose's 'for each label that occurs, any two lattice points carrying that label' names it too, but B collapsed it.

differences.description: A computes the coordinate differences after casting to R with Q first; B computes them in Z and then casts, with p first. B also lists finiteness before positivity. Names and orderings only.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: Rigorous: '$\sqrt{(x_Q-x_P)^2+(y_Q-y_P)^2}$' fixes Q first; the prose gives no order.

rigorous_errors.description: A is faithful to the paraphrase but the resulting left-hand side is unsatisfiable, so the biconditional is false for every admissible c.
rigorous_errors.why_wrong: Honouring 'not necessarily distinct' means taking P = Q, which gives distance 0, and 0 >= c^i is impossible for c > 0. So no labelling exists for any positive c, the left side of the iff is always false, and the iff fails whenever c < sqrt 2. The defect is in the source's parenthetical rather than in A's reading, but the statement is still not provable.

nonrigorous_errors.description: B adds p != q, contradicting the paraphrase's explicit 'not necessarily distinct from each other'.
nonrigorous_errors.why_wrong: The clause was included precisely to make the degenerate case count, and B overrode it. In B's favour, dropping it is the only way to get the intended non-degenerate problem, so B's statement is the sensible one - but it is not what the text says.
nonrigorous_errors.paraphrase_cause: 'any two lattice points carrying that label, not necessarily distinct from each other' - the qualifier trails at the end of a long noun phrase rather than sitting at the quantifier as in '(not necessarily distinct)'.

analysis.paraphrase_effect_summary: Position of a qualifier decided the outcome. The rigorous version's parenthetical sits right at the quantifier and A honoured it - producing the faithful but unsatisfiable statement, since a point at distance 0 from itself cannot exceed c^i. The prose trails the same qualifier at the end of a long noun phrase and B lost it, producing the unfaithful but usable statement. Note the reversal from claude:785, where both wordings dropped the clause: GPT is the more literal transcriber on the symbolic side.

rigorous_paraphrase: Let $\{a_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ be a sequence of nonnegative integers with $a_0 = 1$ and $a_n = a_{n+1} + a_{\lfloor n/3 \rfloor}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$; prove that for every prime $p$ with $p \le 13$, the set $\{n \in \mathbb{N} : p \mid a_n\}$ is infinite.
nonrigorous_paraphrase: Suppose a sequence of nonnegative integers starts with one, and each term equals the next term plus the term whose index is the integer part of one third of the current index; prove that for every prime that does not exceed thirteen, infinitely many terms of the sequence are multiples of that prime.
rigorous_formalization: theorem prime_dvd_sequence_infinitely_often (a : ℕ → ℕ) (ha₀ : a 0 = 1) (hrec : ∀ n : ℕ, a n = a (n + 1) + a (n / 3)) : ∀ p : ℕ, Nat.Prime p → p ≤ 13 → Set.Infinite {n : ℕ | p ∣ a n} := by sorry
nonrigorous_formalization: theorem sequence_prime_multiples (a : ℕ → ℕ) (ha₀ : a 0 = 1) (hrec : ∀ n : ℕ, a (n + 1) = a n + a (n / 3)) : ∀ p : ℕ, Nat.Prime p → p ≤ 13 → ∀ N : ℕ, ∃ n : ℕ, N ≤ n ∧ p ∣ a n := by sorry
reference: theorem proving_zh_blue_1541 (a : ℕ → ℕ) (h₀ : a 0 = 1) (h₁ : ∀ n, a n = a (n + 1) + a ⌊(n / 3 : ℝ)⌋₊) : ∀ p, (Nat.Prime p ∧ p ≤ 13) → {n | p ∣ a n}.Infinite := by sorry

differences.description: A's recurrence is a n = a (n + 1) + a (n / 3), matching the paraphrase. B's is a (n + 1) = a n + a (n / 3), with the direction reversed.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: Rigorous: '$a_n = a_{n+1} + a_{\lfloor n/3 \rfloor}$' shows the three subscripts side by side, so which term is isolated on the left is immediate. Non-rigorous: 'each term equals the next term plus the term whose index is the integer part of one third of the current index' says the same thing, but the direction has to be tracked through a long clause, and B inverted it into the more familiar forward recurrence.

differences.description: A states the conclusion as Set.Infinite {n | p divides a n}; B unfolds it as: for every N there is an n at least N with p dividing a n.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: Rigorous: 'the set $\{n \in \mathbb{N} : p \mid a_n\}$ is infinite' names the set, mapping onto Set.Infinite. Non-rigorous: 'infinitely many terms of the sequence are multiples of that prime' describes the property, and B unfolded it into the equivalent cofinality statement.

differences.description: Theorem names differ: prime_dvd_sequence_infinitely_often versus sequence_prime_multiples.

nonrigorous_errors.description: B reverses the recurrence, writing a (n + 1) = a n + a (n / 3) where the paraphrase says each term equals the next term plus the one-third-index term.
nonrigorous_errors.why_wrong: The two recurrences define completely different sequences. The stated one rearranges to a_(n+1) = a_n - a_(floor n/3), so the sequence is non-increasing and severely constrained by having to stay nonnegative; B's is strictly increasing. The divisibility conclusion is then about a different object entirely.
nonrigorous_errors.paraphrase_cause: 'each term equals the next term plus the term whose index is the integer part of one third of the current index' - a backward recurrence stated in words, where the symbolic version showed the subscripts n, n+1 and floor(n/3) side by side. B normalised it to the more natural forward direction.

analysis.paraphrase_effect_summary: A backward recurrence survived the symbols and was silently normalised by the prose. '$a_n = a_{n+1} + a_{\lfloor n/3 \rfloor}$' is unusual - it defines the sequence going down rather than up - and GPT reproduced it faithfully from the display but flipped it to the familiar forward form when it had to be tracked through a worded clause. The prose did earn one harmless improvement: 'infinitely many terms' unfolded into an explicit cofinality statement rather than Set.Infinite.

rigorous_paraphrase: Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 0}$ and $(b_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be sequences of real numbers. Prove that for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $a_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}b_k$ holds if and only if $b_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^{n-k}\binom{n}{k}a_k$ holds.
nonrigorous_paraphrase: Given two sequences of real numbers indexed by the nonnegative integers, prove that, for each fixed index, the term of the first sequence at that index equals the sum over all indices from zero up to it of the corresponding binomial coefficient times the term of the second sequence exactly when the term of the second sequence at that index equals the analogous sum in which each binomial coefficient times the term of the first sequence is taken with alternating signs, the last term being positive.
rigorous_formalization: theorem binomial_inversion (a b : ℕ → ℝ) : (∀ n : ℕ, a n = ∑ k in Finset.range (n + 1), (Nat.choose n k : ℝ) * b k) ↔ (∀ n : ℕ, b n = ∑ k in Finset.range (n + 1), (-1 : ℝ) ^ (n - k) * (Nat.choose n k : ℝ) * a k) := by sorry
nonrigorous_formalization: theorem binomial_inversion (a b : ℕ → ℝ) : (∀ n : ℕ, a n = ∑ k ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), (Nat.choose n k : ℝ) * b k) ↔ (∀ n : ℕ, b n = ∑ k ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), (-1 : ℝ) ^ (n - k) * (Nat.choose n k : ℝ) * a k) := by sorry
reference: theorem binomial_inversion {a b : ℕ → ℝ} (n : ℕ) : a n = ∑ k ∈ range (n + 1), Nat.choose n k * b k ↔ b n = ∑ k ∈ range (n + 1), (-1) ^ (n - k) * Nat.choose n k * a k := by sorry

differences.description: The two statements are identical except that A uses the deprecated summation binder and B uses the current one. Both carry the same theorem name.

rigorous_errors.description: A quantifies over n inside each side of the biconditional, writing (forall n, a n = ...) <-> (forall n, b n = ...), where the paraphrase puts 'for every $n$' outside the whole equivalence.
rigorous_errors.why_wrong: Read literally the paraphrase asserts a per-index equivalence, which is what the reference encodes and which is false - binomial inversion relates the two sequences as wholes, not index by index. A's reading is the true theorem, so this is a case of the model correcting the source rather than transcribing it, but it is still a deviation from the stated quantifier structure.

rigorous_paraphrase: Let $a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}^{+}$ satisfy $a+b+c=3$; prove that $\frac{a^{4}}{b^{2}+c}+\frac{b^{4}}{c^{2}+a}+\frac{c^{4}}{a^{2}+b}\geq\frac{3}{2}$.
nonrigorous_paraphrase: Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be positive real numbers whose sum is three, and prove that the cyclic sum of the fourth power of $a$ divided by the square of $b$ plus $c$ is at least three halves.
rigorous_formalization: theorem inequality_for_positive_reals (a b c : ℝ) (ha : 0 < a) (hb : 0 < b) (hc : 0 < c) (hsum : a + b + c = 3) : a ^ 4 / (b ^ 2 + c) + b ^ 4 / (c ^ 2 + a) + c ^ 4 / (a ^ 2 + b) ≥ 3 / 2 := by sorry
nonrigorous_formalization: theorem cyclic_fourth_power_inequality (a b c : ℝ) (ha : 0 < a) (hb : 0 < b) (hc : 0 < c) (hsum : a + b + c = 3) : (3 : ℝ) / 2 ≤ a ^ 4 / (b + c) ^ 2 + b ^ 4 / (c + a) ^ 2 + c ^ 4 / (a + b) ^ 2 := by sorry
reference: theorem algebra_335084 (a b c : ℝ) (ha : 0 < a) (hb : 0 < b) (hc : 0 < c) (h : a + b + c = 3) : a ^ 4 / (b ^ 2 + c) + b ^ 4 / (c ^ 2 + a) + c ^ 4 / (a ^ 2 + b) ≥ 3 / 2 := by sorry

differences.paraphrase_evidence: Non-rigorous: 'is at least three halves' reads as a lower bound on the sum, which B rendered with the bound on the left.

differences.description: Theorem names differ: inequality_for_positive_reals versus cyclic_fourth_power_inequality.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: Non-rigorous: 'the cyclic sum of the fourth power' supplies B's name.

nonrigorous_errors.description: B's denominators are (b + c) ^ 2 rather than b ^ 2 + c.

nonrigorous_errors.paraphrase_cause: 'the square of $b$ plus $c$' - a scope ambiguity created purely by writing '$b^{2}+c$' in words.

Two models, same phrase, same wrong reading - this is a reproducible scope ambiguity, and it is especially dangerous because the mis-read statement is itself a plausible true inequality.

rigorous_paraphrase: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$; prove that $f(xf(y))+x=f(x)f(y+1)$ holds for all $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$ if and only if for every $x\in\mathbb{R}$ one has $f(x)=x$ or $f(x)=-x$, so the answer is $f(x)=x$ or $f(x)=-x$.
nonrigorous_paraphrase: Prove that a real-valued function of a real variable has the property that, for every choice of two reals, the value of the function at the product of the first real with the function's value at the second real, increased by the first real, equals the product of the function's value at the first real with its value at one more than the second real, exactly when at every real point the function returns either that point or the negative of that point, so the answer is that the function is the identity or its negative at each point.
rigorous_formalization: theorem functional_equation_iff (f : ℝ → ℝ) : (∀ x y : ℝ, f (x * f y) + x = f x * f (y + 1)) ↔ ((∀ x : ℝ, f x = x) ∨ (∀ x : ℝ, f x = -x)) := by sorry
nonrigorous_formalization: theorem functional_equation_iff (f : ℝ → ℝ) : (∀ x y : ℝ, f (x * f y + x) = f x * f (y + 1)) ↔ (∀ x : ℝ, f x = x ∨ f x = -x) := by sorry
reference: theorem olymid_ref_base_2614 (f : ℝ → ℝ) : (∀ x y, f (x * f y) + x = f x * f (y + 1)) ↔ ∀ x, f x = x ∨ f x = -x := by sorry

differences.description: A's left-hand side is f (x * f y) + x, with the term added outside the function. B's is f (x * f y + x), with the term moved inside the argument.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: Non-rigorous: 'the value of the function at the product of the first real with the function's value at the second real, increased by the first real'. 'Increased by the first real' can modify the value or the argument, and B attached it to the argument. The symbolic '$f(xf(y))+x$' is unambiguous.

differences.description: A's right-hand side is ((forall x, f x = x) or (forall x, f x = -x)); B's is the pointwise (forall x, f x = x or f x = -x).
differences.paraphrase_evidence: Rigorous: 'for every $x\in\mathbb{R}$ one has $f(x)=x$ or $f(x)=-x$' detaches the quantifier and lets the disjunction float. Non-rigorous: 'at every real point the function returns either that point or the negative of that point' binds them together, and B kept it pointwise.

differences.description: Both theorems carry the same name, functional_equation_iff.

rigorous_errors.description: A hoists the disjunction above the quantifier.
rigorous_errors.why_wrong: The paraphrase's condition is pointwise, so A's version is strictly stronger and excludes functions that are the identity somewhere and the negation elsewhere.
rigorous_errors.paraphrase_cause: 'for every $x\in\mathbb{R}$ one has $f(x)=x$ or $f(x)=-x$' - the detached leading quantifier invited the hoist.

nonrigorous_errors.description: B's left-hand side is f (x * f y + x) instead of f (x * f y) + x.
nonrigorous_errors.why_wrong: The added x belongs outside the function application, not inside its argument. B's equation constrains a different relation, so the classification on the right no longer characterises it.
nonrigorous_errors.paraphrase_cause: 'increased by the first real' - the modifier's attachment point is lost once the parentheses of '$f(xf(y))+x$' are gone, and B resolved it inward.

analysis.paraphrase_effect_summary: Complementary failures, and instructive against Claude on the same problem. GPT's symbolic version hoisted the disjunction just as Claude's did (claude:839), but where Claude's prose version parsed the nested left-hand side correctly, GPT's pulled 'increased by the first real' inside the argument. So the same 'increased by' ambiguity is resolved differently by different models - outward for Claude, inward for GPT - which means the phrasing is unreliable rather than systematically biased in one direction.

rigorous_paraphrase: Prove that $\sum_{k=1}^{4} \binom{10}{k}\binom{10-k}{5-k} = 7560$, i.e. the number of ways to choose a committee of $5$ people from $10$ distinguishable people together with a nonempty set of $k$ committee leaders inside it, where $1 \le k \le 4$, is $7560$. Show that the answer is $7560$.
nonrigorous_paraphrase: Ten distinguishable people wish to form a committee of five of themselves by first electing a group of leaders numbering at least one and at most four, who then fill the remaining committee seats from the people not elected as leaders; counting two committees with the same members but different groups of leaders as different, find the number of ways the committee can be formed. Show that the answer is $7560$.
rigorous_formalization: theorem committee_with_leaders_count : (∑ k in Finset.Icc (1 : ℕ) 4, Nat.choose 10 k * Nat.choose (10 - k) (5 - k)) = 7560 := by sorry
nonrigorous_formalization: theorem committee_formation_count : Nat.card {p : Finset (Fin 10) × Finset (Fin 10) // 1 ≤ p.1.1.card ∧ p.1.1.card ≤ 4 ∧ p.1.1 ⊆ p.1.2 ∧ p.1.2.card = 5} = 7560 := by sorry
reference: theorem omni_theorem_1218 : ∑ k ∈ ({1, 2, 3, 4} : Set ℕ), Nat.choose 10 k * Nat.choose (10 - k) (5 - k) = 7560 := by sorry

differences.description: A transcribes the closed-form sum, proving that the sum over k from 1 to 4 of C(10,k) * C(10-k,5-k) equals 7560. B builds the combinatorial object instead, counting pairs consisting of a leader set of size 1 to 4 contained in a five-member committee.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: Rigorous: 'Prove that $\sum_{k=1}^{4} \binom{10}{k}\binom{10-k}{5-k} = 7560$' hands over the formula and only then glosses the combinatorics, so A had an identity to transcribe. Non-rigorous: 'first electing a group of leaders numbering at least one and at most four, who then fill the remaining committee seats' plus 'counting two committees with the same members but different groups of leaders as different' supplies only the narrative, so B had to model the set of outcomes - which is the more faithful formalization of the counting problem.

differences.description: B's subtype projections are one level too deep: the predicate binds p at type Finset (Fin 10) x Finset (Fin 10), so p.1 is already the first component and p.1.1, p.1.2 reach into Finset's underlying multiset and its nodup proof.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: A knock-on of the encoding choice above: only B needed a product type in the first place, because only B was modelling the outcome set rather than transcribing a sum.

differences.description: Theorem names differ: committee_with_leaders_count versus committee_formation_count. A also uses the deprecated summation binder.

The conditions p.1.1 subseteq p.1.2 and p.1.2.card = 5 therefore do not typecheck at all. The modelling is right - a leader set of size between 1 and 4 contained in a five-element committee is exactly the outcome the prose describes - and only the projection depth is wrong.

The rigorous version supplied the sum, so A never needed a product type.

analysis.paraphrase_effect_summary: The interesting case where the prose asked for more and got closer to the real problem. A merely verifies the arithmetic identity its paraphrase handed it, which is faithful but sidesteps the combinatorics; B modelled the outcome set directly, exactly as the narrative describes, and would have been the better formalization - but botched the subtype projections, writing p.1.1 and p.1.2 for p.1 and p.2, so its statement does not typecheck. Handing the model a formula avoids modelling risk at the cost of not formalizing the question.

rigorous_paraphrase: Let $n \geq 0$ be an integer and let $a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_n$ be real numbers; show that there exists $k \in \{0, 1, \ldots, n\}$ such that $\sum_{i=0}^{n} a_i x^i \leq \sum_{i=0}^{k} a_i$ for all real $x \in [0,1]$.
nonrigorous_paraphrase: Take any nonempty finite list of real numbers, and read it as the coefficients of a polynomial listed in order of increasing degree, beginning with the constant term; show that some nonempty initial segment of that list has a total that is at least the value of the polynomial at every point of the closed unit interval.
rigorous_formalization: theorem polynomial_bounded_by_partial_sum (n : ℕ) (a : ℕ → ℝ) : ∃ k ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), ∀ x ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1, (∑ i ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), a i * x ^ i) ≤ ∑ i ∈ Finset.range (k + 1), a i := by sorry
nonrigorous_formalization: theorem exists_initial_segment_sum_ge_polynomial (a : List ℝ) (ha : a ≠ []) : ∃ n : ℕ, 0 < n ∧ n ≤ a.length ∧ ∀ x ∈ Set.Icc (-1 : ℝ) 1, (a.enum.map (fun p => p.2 * x ^ p.1)).sum ≤ (a.take n).sum := by sorry
reference: theorem olymid_ref_base_1179 (n : ℕ) (a : ℕ → ℝ) : ∃ k ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), ∀ x ∈ Icc 0 1, ∑ i in Finset.range (n + 1), a i * x ^ i ≤ ∑ i in Finset.range (k + 1), a i := by sorry

differences.description: A quantifies x over Set.Icc 0 1; B quantifies it over Set.Icc (-1) 1.

differences.description: A models the coefficients as a function from N to R together with a degree bound n, taking sums over Finset.range. B models them as a List R with a nonemptiness hypothesis, pairing coefficients with exponents via List.enum and taking initial segments with List.take.

analysis.paraphrase_effect_summary: Naming a standard interval instead of printing its endpoints cost the problem its truth. '$x \in [0,1]$' transcribes mechanically; 'the closed unit interval' had to be resolved, and GPT resolved it as [-1, 1], which makes the statement false with a two-coefficient counterexample. Note the prose was otherwise the more careful reading - it modelled the coefficients as an actual finite list with enum-indexed exponents and stated the nonemptiness of the initial segment explicitly, all of which matches the wording better than A's infinite coefficient family.

differences.description: A defines the assignment by an explicit sum over bit positions, testing each bit of the argument and contributing the corresponding power. differences.paraphrase_evidence: Rigorous: 'for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ whose binary representation is $n = \sum_{i=0}^{m} a_i 2^i$ ... the value $p_n = \sum_{i=0}^{m} a_i q^i$' prints a sum over digits, and A produced a sum over bits. Non-rigorous: 'taking the binary digits of $n$ and reading that same digit string in base $q$ instead of base two' describes the operation on digit strings, and B extracted the two shift rules that operation satisfies. The recurrences are correct - appending a zero bit multiplies by the base, appending a one bit multiplies and adds one - and they pin the assignment uniquely by strong induction, so the two encodings define the same function.

analysis.paraphrase_effect_summary: Both correct and equivalent, and B's recursive characterisation is the notable artefact: describing the assignment as re-reading a digit string in a new base, rather than printing the digit sum, led GPT to derive the two functional equations that the operation satisfies and to define the object by them. That is a genuine mathematical step taken during formalization, it is correct, and it produces the statement a prover would rather have. A's bit-sum version is also correct, including its choice of a safe over-bound on the number of bit positions.

rigorous_paraphrase: Let $c$ be an integer with $c \ge 0$, and let $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots$ be a sequence of integers such that $a_n > 0$ for every integer $n \ge 0$ and such that for every integer $n \ge 0$ the value $a_n$ equals the number of indices $i \ge 1$ satisfying $a_i \le a_{n+1} + c$; prove that $a_n = n + c + 1$ for every integer $n \ge 0$.

analysis.paraphrase_effect_summary: Both correct and equivalent, and both make the same improvement on the reference, independently: they conjoin the finiteness of the counted set to the counting hypothesis. That matters because the cardinality function returns zero on an infinite set, so without the conjunct the hypothesis silently means something else whenever the set is unbounded. Adding it makes both statements formally weaker than the reference - it is an extra assumption - but it is the only reading under which the hypothesis says what the problem says.

rigorous_paraphrase: Let $a, b$ be integers with $a > 2$ and $b > 2$. Prove that there exist a positive integer $k$ and positive integers $n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k$ such that $n_1 = a$, $n_k = b$, and $(n_i + n_{i+1}) \mid n_i n_{i+1}$ for every $i = 1, 2, \ldots, k-1$.

differences.paraphrase_evidence: Rigorous: 'there exist a positive integer $k$ and positive integers $n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k$ such that $n_1 = a$, $n_k = b$, and $(n_i + n_{i+1}) \mid n_i n_{i+1}$ for every $i = 1, 2, \ldots, k-1$' gives subscripts and an index range. Non-rigorous: 'one can pass from the first to the second by a finite chain of positive integers, beginning at the first number and ending at the second, in which the sum of any two neighbouring terms always divides their product' names a chain with a beginning, an end and neighbours, and B used exactly the dependently-typed constructions for those three notions.

analysis.paraphrase_effect_summary: Both correct and equivalent, and both improve on the reference, which requires positivity only for indices up to one less than the length - so the final term of its chain need not be positive - and which guards the divisibility by an interval computed with a truncated subtraction. B's version is the most robust of the three: adjacency is expressed by the successor embedding on a finite type, so no index can fall outside the chain and no arithmetic on indices appears at all. The prose words 'chain', 'beginning', 'ending' and 'neighbouring' map one-for-one onto those constructions.

B's is the tighter statement: A has to assert coprimality and positivity and to pin the quotient, three conditions that could in principle be stated inconsistently, whereas B's projections cannot be. Both correctly restrict to the open unit interval, which is what makes the numerator smaller than the denominator and gives the answer 128 rather than twice that.

rigorous_paraphrase: Let $b, s_1, s_2, s_3$ be natural numbers such that $\frac{s_1+s_2+s_3}{3} = 27$ and $\frac{b+s_1+s_2+s_3}{4} = 28$; find $b$. Prove that the answer is $31$.

analysis.paraphrase_effect_summary: Both correct and equivalent, and both repair a reference that is false. The reference performs both divisions in the naturals, so its hypotheses say only that the sisters' total lies between eighty-one and eighty-three and that the four-person total lies between one hundred twelve and one hundred fifteen; the age it concludes is then not determined - a total of eighty-two with an age of thirty satisfies both hypotheses and refutes the conclusion. A escapes by casting into the rationals and B by clearing the denominators, and each of those is sufficient on its own.

analysis.paraphrase_effect_summary: Both correct: the ten qualifying integers are two, eleven, twenty, one hundred one, one hundred ten, two hundred, one thousand one, one thousand ten, one thousand one hundred and two thousand, and their squares sum to exactly 7294927. The wording effect is a small illustration of a general cost: choosing the integers because the display said 'integers' forces a conversion at every use of a natural-number-only library function, and the conversion is sound only under a range hypothesis that the statement does not tie to it.

differences.description: Both use set cardinality where the reference uses the extended-natural cardinality. A omits the tactic block before the placeholder proof. Theorem names differ.

analysis.paraphrase_effect_summary: Both correct and equivalent, and both repair a reference that is false. The reference divides twice the product by the sum in the naturals, so its condition is that the truncated quotient equals the target - which admits every pair whose exact harmonic mean lies in a unit interval above the target, strictly more pairs than the equation allows, so its cardinality exceeds the asserted 799. The two branches escaped by different routes: the rigorous one cleared the denominator, the prose one moved to the rationals because the definition it was handed is built from reciprocals. Either route suffices, and it is notable that the paraphrase which never mentions a fraction is the one that ended up computing in a field.

The reference omits the parallelism entirely, so its four points need not form a trapezoid at all; the sought length is the difference of squares of a diagonal and a leg, which without parallelism is unconstrained, so its conclusion does not follow. rigorous_errors.description: The statement is false: no such function exists. Its first two conditions pin the function to be the indicator of the rationals, and the third then requires every positive real to be a period of that indicator, which fails - taking the period to be the square root of two and the argument zero gives value zero at the shifted point against value one at the origin.
rigorous_errors.why_wrong: The indicator of the rationals is periodic exactly with rational periods. An irrational period would carry the origin, where the value is one, to an irrational point, where the value is zero. So the conjunction of the three conditions is unsatisfiable and the existential claim is false. Only the fourth condition, the absence of a smallest positive period, is a genuine property of the function - the positive rationals have no least element.
rigorous_errors.paraphrase_cause: Inherited. The reference asserts periodicity for every positive real as well, and the rigorous paraphrase transcribes exactly that - 'D(x+c)=D(x) for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$ and every real $c>0$'. The intended problem is almost certainly about rational periods; the quantifier was already wrong before the paraphrase step.

rigorous_errors.description: Consequence of the same defect: the fourth condition is stated about the set of all positive periods, which under the third condition would be all positive reals and would indeed have no least element - so the two conditions are not independently contradictory, but the third alone is unsatisfiable.
rigorous_errors.why_wrong: Recorded separately only to note that the statement's falsity comes from the periodicity quantifier and not from the minimality clause, which is the interesting half of the problem.

rigorous_paraphrase: Let $k \in \mathbb{N}$ with $1 \le k \le 1986$, and let a subset $S \subseteq \{1,2,\dots,1986\}$ with $|S| = k$ be chosen uniformly at random among all $\binom{1986}{k}$ such subsets; players $A$, $B$, $C$ win according as $\sum_{x \in S} x \equiv 0, 1, 2 \pmod 3$ respectively. Prove that the game is fair, i.e. each of the three events has probability $\frac{1}{3}$, if and only if $k = 660$ or $k = 1320$.

Prove that the game is fair, meaning that each of the three players wins with probability one third, exactly when $k$ is six hundred sixty or one thousand three hundred twenty.

The two are inter-derivable, since two integer polynomials agreeing at every integer are equal, but they are not the same proposition and only A expresses the factorisation the problem asks for.

The resulting theorem is a true arithmetic identity that a ring-normalisation tactic closes immediately, and it says nothing about divisibility in the polynomial ring - which is the content of a factorisation problem.

analysis.paraphrase_effect_summary: Both correct and equivalent. The answer is forced by two congruences - the value at zero is congruent to one hundred forty-five modulo ten and to one hundred sixty-four modulo nine, so it lies in a single residue class modulo ninety, whose smallest absolute value is twenty-five, attained at minus twenty-five. The 'value at zero' against 'constant term' mapping is the same kind of lexical-to-API effect as gcd against coprimality and formula against library name.

The defect originates in the reference, which performs the subtraction on naturals, and the paraphrase step turned an encoding artefact into a stipulated convention.

rigorous_formalization: theorem find_w (x y z w : ℝ) (h₁ : 2 * x + y + z + w = 1) (h₂ : x + 3 * y + z + w = 2) (h₃ : x + y + 4 * z + w = 3) (h₄ : x + y + z + 5 * w = 25) : w = 11 / 2 := by sorry
nonrigorous_formalization: theorem fourth_number_is_eleven_halves (a b c d : ℝ) (h₁ : (a + b + c + d) + a = 1) (h₂ : (a + b + c + d) + 2 * b = 2) (h₃ : (a + b + c + d) + 3 * c = 3) (h₄ : (a + b + c + d) + 4 * d = 25) : d = 11 / 2 := by sorry
reference: theorem olymid_ref_base_7217 (x y z w : ℝ) (h₀ : 2 * x + y + z + w = 1) (h₁ : x + 3 * y + z + w = 2) (h₂ : x + y + 4 * z + w = 3) (h₃ : x + y + z + 5 * w = 25) : w = 11 / 2 := by sorry

differences.description: A transcribes the four equations with collected coefficients (2x+y+z+w=1, x+3y+z+w=2, ...), matching the reference. B writes each hypothesis as the total of all four plus a multiple of one of them: (a+b+c+d)+a=1, (a+b+c+d)+2b=2, (a+b+c+d)+3c=3, (a+b+c+d)+4d=25. Expanding B's gives A's exactly, so the systems are identical.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: The rigorous text prints the collected form '$2x+y+z+w=1$'; the prose states 'their total plus the first equals one, their total plus twice the second equals two, ...'. The paraphraser performed the decomposition into total-plus-multiple, and B transcribed that decomposition literally.

differences.description: Variables x y z w vs a b c d; hypothesis and theorem names differ; A asks for w, B for d.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: The rigorous text names the unknowns $x,y,z,w$; the prose speaks of numbers 'listed in order as first, second, third and fourth', so B used a b c d and concluded about d.

analysis.paraphrase_effect_summary: A clean case of the paraphraser doing algebra: rewriting the collected coefficients as 'total plus a multiple' is a mathematical step taken in the prose paraphrase, not in the formalizer, and B faithfully reproduced it. Cross-model reproducibility: claude:877 is the same source problem and Claude's prose branch produced the same total-plus-multiple split, so this wording effect is model-independent.

rigorous_paraphrase: Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n$ be positive real numbers with $x_1x_2\cdots x_n=1$; prove that $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{x_i(1+x_i)}\ge\frac{n}{2}$.
nonrigorous_paraphrase: Given a nonempty finite list of positive real numbers whose product equals one, prove that the sum, taken over all the numbers in the list, of the reciprocal of the product of a number with one more than itself is at least half the number of terms in the list.
rigorous_formalization: theorem sum_reciprocal_product_bound (n : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) (x : Fin n → ℝ) (hx : ∀ i, 0 < x i) (hprod : ∏ i, x i = 1) : ∑ i, 1 / (x i * (1 + x i)) ≥ (n : ℝ) / 2 := by sorry
nonrigorous_formalization: theorem reciprocal_product_sum_bound (xs : List ℝ) (hne : xs ≠ []) (hpos : ∀ x ∈ xs, 0 < x) (hprod : xs.prod = 1) : (xs.map (fun x => 1 / (x * (x + 1)))).sum ≥ (xs.length : ℝ) / 2 := by sorry
reference: theorem algebra_58273 {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) (x : Fin n → ℝ) (hx : ∀ i, 0 < x i) (hxp : ∏ i, x i = 1) : ∑ i, (1 / (x i * (1 + x i))) ≥ n / 2 := by sorry

differences.description: A uses an indexed family x : Fin n -> R with 0 < n, Finset.prod and Finset.sum, exactly as the reference. B uses xs : List R with hne : xs != [], List.prod, (xs.map _).sum and xs.length. Equivalent statements of the same inequality.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: Rigorous: 'let $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n$ be positive real numbers' - an indexed family, which A and the reference mirror. Non-rigorous: 'Given a nonempty finite list of positive real numbers' - the words 'list' and 'nonempty' map directly onto List and xs != [], and 'the number of terms in the list' onto xs.length.

differences.description: A writes the summand as 1 / (x i * (1 + x i)) with the 1 first; B as 1 / (x * (x + 1)).
differences.paraphrase_evidence: Rigorous prints '$\frac{1}{x_i(1+x_i)}$'; the prose says 'the reciprocal of the product of a number with one more than itself', which puts the number first.

differences.description: Theorem and hypothesis names differ; A casts (n : R) / 2 explicitly where the reference leaves the coercion implicit.

analysis.paraphrase_effect_summary: The list cue fires again, and cleanly: the single word 'list' in the prose moved the whole statement off Fin n and onto the List API, including the nonemptiness hypothesis and the length. This is now the eighth or ninth instance (claude:658, 659, 888; gpt:25, 44, 99, 123) and is among the most reliable wording effects in the corpus.

rigorous_paraphrase: Let $k>0$ be a real number, and for each positive integer $n$ let $P_n=(n,nk)$ be a point in the plane. Suppose there exist positive integers $m$ and $n$ with $|m-n|=4$ such that $\sqrt{(m-n)^2+(mk-nk)^2}=31$. Prove that $\sqrt{(7-19)^2+(7k-19k)^2}=93$, i.e. show that the answer is $93$.
nonrigorous_paraphrase: Arpon picks a positive real number and, for every positive integer, places a marker at the point whose first coordinate is that integer and whose second coordinate is that integer times his chosen number; given that some two of these markers whose first coordinates differ by four are exactly thirty-one apart, show that the distance between the markers belonging to seven and to nineteen is $93$.
rigorous_formalization: theorem distance_between_points_eq_93 (k : ℝ) (hk : 0 < k) (h : ∃ m n : ℤ, 0 < m ∧ 0 < n ∧ |m - n| = 4 ∧ Real.sqrt (((m : ℝ) - (n : ℝ)) ^ 2 + ((m : ℝ) * k - (n : ℝ) * k) ^ 2) = 31) : Real.sqrt (((7 : ℝ) - 19) ^ 2 + (7 * k - 19 * k) ^ 2) = 93 := by sorry
nonrigorous_formalization: theorem arpon_marker_distance (x : ℝ) (hx : 0 < x) (h : ∃ m n : ℕ, 0 < m ∧ 0 < n ∧ |(m : ℝ) - (n : ℝ)| = 4 ∧ Real.sqrt (((m : ℝ) - (n : ℝ)) ^ 2 + ((m : ℝ) * x - (n : ℝ) * x) ^ 2) = 31) : Real.sqrt (((19 : ℝ) - 7) ^ 2 + ((19 : ℝ) * x - (7 : ℝ) * x) ^ 2) = 93 := by sorry
reference: theorem olymid_ref_base_4365 (k : ℝ) (hk : k > 0) (h : ∃ m n, m > 0 ∧ n > 0 ∧ m ≠ n ∧ |(m : ℝ) - n| = 4 ∧ Real.sqrt ((m - n)^2 + (m * k - n * k)^2) = 31) : Real.sqrt ((7 - 19)^2 + (7 * k - 19 * k)^2) = 93 := by sorry

differences.description: A quantifies the two witnesses over Z (exists m n : Z) and takes the absolute difference in Z: |m - n| = 4. B quantifies over N and casts both to R before taking the absolute value: |(m:R) - (n:R)| = 4. Both are sound, but for different reasons: A's abs is the integer one on a total subtraction, while B's cast to R is what rescues it - written as |m - n| = 4 in N, truncated subtraction would have turned the condition into max(m,n) - min(m,n) >= 4 collapsing wrongly (in fact into 'm - n = 4 or n - m = 4' only by accident of the abs being unavailable in N at all).
differences.paraphrase_evidence: Rigorous: 'Suppose there exist positive integers $m$ and $n$ with $|m-n|=4$' - printed integers and a printed absolute value, so A took the domain where subtraction is total. Non-rigorous: 'some two of these markers whose first coordinates differ by four' describes integer labels of markers, and B chose N, then had to cast into R for the difference to mean anything.

differences.description: A's conclusion squares (7 - 19) and (7k - 19k); B squares (19 - 7) and (19x - 7x). Identical after squaring.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: The rigorous text prints '$\sqrt{(7-19)^2+(7k-19k)^2}=93$' and A copies the order; the prose gives no formula ('the distance between the markers belonging to seven and to nineteen'), and B wrote each difference in the order that makes it positive.

differences.description: A keeps the name k for the slope; B renames it x ('Arpon picks a positive real number'). Both drop the reference's redundant m != n, which |m-n|=4 already implies.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: The prose never names the chosen number, so B picked a neutral x; the rigorous text calls it $k$.

analysis.paraphrase_effect_summary: A domain difference driven by the wording (printed integers and a printed absolute value versus 'coordinates that differ by four') that happens to be harmless, but only because the prose branch cast into R before taking the absolute value. Verified the mathematics: |m-n|=4 with distance 31 forces 4*sqrt(1+k^2) = 31, and the 7-to-19 distance is 12*sqrt(1+k^2) = 3*31 = 93, so both statements are true.

rigorous_paraphrase: Prove that there are no real numbers $x,y,z,t$ satisfying all four of $|x|>|y-z+t|$, $|y|>|x-z+t|$, $|z|>|x-y+t|$, and $|t|>|x-y+z|$.
nonrigorous_paraphrase: Given four real numbers, listed in a fixed order, prove that it is impossible for each of them to have absolute value strictly greater than the absolute value of the alternating sum of the other three taken in their original order beginning with a plus sign.
rigorous_formalization: theorem no_reals_satisfy_abs_inequalities : ¬ ∃ x y z t : ℝ, |x| > |y - z + t| ∧ |y| > |x - z + t| ∧ |z| > |x - y + t| ∧ |t| > |x - y + z| := by sorry
nonrigorous_formalization: theorem impossible_absolute_value_inequalities (a b c d : ℝ) : ¬ (|a| > |b - c + d| ∧ |b| > |a - c + d| ∧ |c| > |a - b + d| ∧ |d| > |a - b + c|) := by sorry
reference: theorem algebra_585850 (x y z t : ℝ) : (|x| > |y - z + t| ∧ |y| > |x - z + t| ∧ |z| > |x - y + t| ∧ |t| > |x - y + z|) ↔ False := by sorry

differences.description: A states the impossibility as a closed negated existential: not exists x y z t : R, (four inequalities). B takes the four reals as theorem parameters and negates the conjunction: not (|a| > |b-c+d| and ...). The reference uses a third form, (four inequalities) iff False. All three are equivalent.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: Rigorous: 'Prove that there are no real numbers $x,y,z,t$ satisfying all four' - an explicit non-existence, which A rendered as not exists. Non-rigorous: 'Given four real numbers, listed in a fixed order, prove that it is impossible for each of them to ...' - the numbers are given first and the impossibility asserted of them, which is exactly B's parameters-plus-negation shape.

differences.description: Variables x y z t vs a b c d; theorem names differ.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: The rigorous text names them $x,y,z,t$; the prose names nothing, so B used a b c d.

analysis.paraphrase_effect_summary: The wording effect is real but weak, and the control matters: this direction (printed non-existence -> not exists, prose 'impossible for given numbers' -> parameters plus negation) matches gpt:74 but is the reverse of claude:787, where Claude's rigorous branch got the universally quantified form and the prose branch the negated existential. Two consistent GPT instances against one opposite Claude instance suggests a per-model house style rather than a stable wording effect, so this category should not be counted as evidence without more data.

rigorous_paraphrase: The sum of all positive integers $m$ for which $\frac{13!}{m}$ is a perfect square can be written as $2^a3^b5^c7^d11^e13^f$ with $a,b,c,d,e,f$ positive integers; find $a+b+c+d+e+f$. Prove that the answer is $12$.
nonrigorous_paraphrase: Add up every positive integer that divides the factorial of thirteen leaving a perfect square as the quotient; this total can be written as a product of powers of the primes two, three, five, seven, eleven and thirteen, each with a positive exponent, and the task is to find the sum of those six exponents. Prove that the answer is $12$.
rigorous_formalization: theorem factorial_13_square_quotient_exponents : ∃ a b c d e f : ℕ, 0 < a ∧ 0 < b ∧ 0 < c ∧ 0 < d ∧ 0 < e ∧ 0 < f ∧ (∑ m in (Nat.factorial 13).divisors, if ∃ k : ℕ, Nat.factorial 13 / m = k ^ 2 then m else 0) = 2 ^ a * 3 ^ b * 5 ^ c * 7 ^ d * 11 ^ e * 13 ^ f ∧ a + b + c + d + e + f = 12 := by sorry
nonrigorous_formalization: theorem sum_divisors_of_factorial_thirteen_with_square_quotient : ∃ a2 a3 a5 a7 a11 a13 : ℕ, 0 < a2 ∧ 0 < a3 ∧ 0 < a5 ∧ 0 < a7 ∧ 0 < a11 ∧ 0 < a13 ∧ (∑ d in (Nat.factorial 13).divisors.filter (fun d => Nat.sqrt (Nat.factorial 13 / d) ^ 2 = Nat.factorial 13 / d), d) = 2 ^ a2 * 3 ^ a3 * 5 ^ a5 * 7 ^ a7 * 11 ^ a11 * 13 ^ a13 ∧ a2 + a3 + a5 + a7 + a11 + a13 = 12 := by sorry
reference: theorem aime_all_2023_I_4 (s : Set ℕ) (hs : s = { m > 0 | IsSquare (Nat.factorial 13 / m) }) (a b c d e f : ℕ) (ha : 0 < a) (hb : 0 < b) (hc : 0 < c) (hd : 0 < d) (he : 0 < e) (hf : 0 < f) (h : ∑ᶠ m ∈ s, m = 2 ^ a * 3 ^ b * 5 ^ c * 7 ^ d * 11 ^ e * 13 ^ f) : a + b + c + d + e + f = 12 := by sorry

differences.description: A tests squareness with an unbounded existential inside an if-then-else summand: sum over (13!).divisors of (if exists k : N, 13!/m = k^2 then m else 0). B filters the divisor finset with the computable predicate Nat.sqrt (13!/d)^2 = 13!/d and sums the survivors. The two tests are mathematically the same, but only B's is decidable by instance (see the rigorous error).
differences.paraphrase_evidence: Both wordings say 'perfect square' outright ('$\frac{13!}{m}$ is a perfect square' vs 'leaving a perfect square as the quotient'), and neither hints at an integer square root, so B's computable encoding is the model's own choice rather than a wording effect. It nevertheless decides whether the statement elaborates.

differences.description: Both branches restrict the sum to (Nat.factorial 13).divisors, where the reference sums over the set {m > 0 | IsSquare (13! / m)}. This is a shared repair of a genuine reference defect, not a difference between the branches.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: Neither paraphrase mentions divisibility in the rigorous case ('all positive integers $m$ for which $13!/m$ is a perfect square'), while the prose does say 'every positive integer that divides the factorial of thirteen'. Both branches restricted to divisors anyway, so the prose's extra word was not needed. The reference's defect: 13!/m is truncated natural division, so every m > 13! gives 13!/m = 0 = 0^2 and lies in the set; the set is therefore infinite, its finsum has no finite support and evaluates to 0, and the reference's hypothesis becomes 0 = 2^a*3^b*5^c*7^d*11^e*13^f with all six exponents positive - unsatisfiable. The reference is vacuously true.

differences.description: Both branches convert the reference's hypothesis-style exponent equation into an existential over the six exponents, asserting that such a representation exists with positive exponents summing to 12. Given unique factorization this is equivalent to the reference's intent. Same on both branches.

rigorous_errors.description: A's summand 'if exists k : N, Nat.factorial 13 / m = k ^ 2 then m else 0' has no Decidable instance, so the statement does not elaborate.
rigorous_errors.why_wrong: Finset.sum over an if-then-else requires Decidable for the condition, and 'exists k : N, ...' is an unbounded existential for which Mathlib provides no decision procedure. The universal fallback Classical.propDecidable is declared 'noncomputable scoped instance (priority := low)' in Lean core (Init/Classical.lean line 79, toolchain v4.28.0), so it is in scope only after 'open Classical'; the extracted preamble for this statement is just 'import Mathlib'. Checked against Mathlib rev 8f9d9cff6b. B is immune because Nat.sqrt (13!/d)^2 = 13!/d is a decidable equality of naturals.

It is recorded because it means the statement does not elaborate against the checkout used here, not because the mathematics is wrong.

analysis.paraphrase_effect_summary: Both branches independently repaired a vacuous reference (the reference's unrestricted set is infinite, so its finsum is the junk value 0 and its hypotheses are contradictory), and both assert the true arithmetic: the sum of the divisors leaving a square quotient is 9698458770 = 2 * 3^2 * 5 * 7^3 * 11 * 13^4, whose exponents sum to 12 (verified by enumerating all 792 divisors of 13!). The one asymmetry is not mathematical but a well-formedness accident: the rigorous branch's existential squareness test is undecidable by instance and does not elaborate, while the prose branch's Nat.sqrt round trip is computable. Not caused by the wording, but a reminder that the choice of squareness encoding is load-bearing for compilability.

rigorous_paraphrase: For $x \in \mathbb{R}$ let $I(x) = \int_{-0.4}^{0.2} (1.5 t^{3} - 1.0 t + 0.4)\, e^{x(-0.4 t^{3} - 2.7 \arctan t + 1.6)}\, dt$; prove that $\lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{I(x)}{0.28 e^{2.65 x}/x} = 1$, so that the answer is $I(x) \approx \dfrac{0.28 e^{2.65 x}}{x}$.
nonrigorous_paraphrase: For each real number $x$, let $I(x)$ be the integral, with respect to $t$ over the interval from minus four tenths to two tenths, of the product of the cubic polynomial whose value at $t$ is one and a half times the cube of $t$, minus $t$, plus four tenths, with the exponential of $x$ times the quantity obtained by taking one and six tenths, subtracting four tenths of the cube of $t$, and subtracting twenty-seven tenths of the arctangent of $t$; prove that as $x$ grows without bound the ratio of $I(x)$ to twenty-eight hundredths times the exponential of two and sixty-five hundredths times $x$, all divided by $x$, tends to one, so that the answer is $I(x) \approx \dfrac{0.28 e^{2.65 x}}{x}$.
rigorous_formalization: theorem integral_asymptotic : Filter.Tendsto (fun x : ℝ => (∫ t : ℝ in (-0.4)..0.2, (1.5 * t ^ 3 - 1.0 * t + 0.4) * Real.exp (x * (-0.4 * t ^ 3 - 2.7 * Real.arctan t + 1.6))) / (0.28 * Real.exp (2.65 * x) / x)) Filter.atTop (𝓝 1) := by sorry
nonrigorous_formalization: theorem integral_asymptotic : Tendsto (fun x : ℝ => (∫ t in (-2 / 5 : ℝ)..(1 / 5 : ℝ), ((3 / 2 : ℝ) * t ^ 3 - t + 2 / 5) * Real.exp (x * ((8 / 5 : ℝ) - (2 / 5) * t ^ 3 - (27 / 10) * Real.arctan t))) / (((7 / 25 : ℝ) * Real.exp ((53 / 20 : ℝ) * x)) / x)) atTop (𝓝 (1 : ℝ)) := by sorry
reference: theorem hardmath_91 (I : ℝ → ℝ) (hI : I = λ x => ∫ t in (-0.4)..0.2, (1.5*t^3 - 1.0*t + 0.4)*exp (x * (-0.4*t^3 - 2.7*arctan t + 1.6))) : Tendsto (λ x => I x / (0.28 * exp (2.65 * x) / x)) atTop (𝓝 1) := by sorry

differences.description: A keeps every constant as the printed decimal (-0.4, 0.2, 1.5, 1.0, 2.7, 1.6, 0.28, 2.65). B converts each to an exact fraction (-2/5, 1/5, 3/2, 8/5, 27/10, 7/25, 53/20) and drops the redundant coefficient 1.0 from the 't' term. Every conversion is exact (0.28 = 7/25 and 2.65 = 53/20 in particular, both verified), and Lean's decimal literals in R are exact rationals via OfScientific rather than floats, so the two statements are literally the same real numbers.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: The rigorous text prints decimals; the prose spells every constant out in words - 'four tenths', 'one and a half', 'one and six tenths', 'twenty-seven tenths', 'twenty-eight hundredths', 'two and sixty-five hundredths'. Verbalizing the decimals is what produced fractions on the prose branch: B rendered each spoken fraction as the fraction it names.

differences.description: A writes the exponent in the printed order, x * (-0.4*t^3 - 2.7*arctan t + 1.6). B writes x * (8/5 - (2/5)*t^3 - (27/10)*arctan t), constant first. Same expression.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: The prose dictates B's order explicitly: 'taking one and six tenths, subtracting four tenths of the cube of $t$, and subtracting twenty-seven tenths of the arctangent of $t$'.

differences.description: Both branches inline the integral into the limit instead of reifying I as a function with a defining hypothesis, as the reference does. Same on both branches.
differences.paraphrase_evidence: Notable as a non-firing of the naming cue: both paraphrases do name the object ('let $I(x) = \int ...$' and 'let $I(x)$ be the integral'), and the reference carries I as a parameter, yet neither branch reified it. The reification effect seen elsewhere in the corpus is therefore not automatic on a named integral.
